children: A former investment advisor and broker has been sentenced to more than seven years in prison for stealing nearly $10 million from an elderly client. Ejiroghene Okuma, 44, of Smyrna, Ga., pleaded guilty to one count of wire fraud in March.

Prosecutors say that Okuma began embezzling money from his client in March 2022. The previous month, he had been appointed to administer the estate of the victim's sister. He falsely told the client that he would need funds to manage the estate and under that pretense stole about $900,000.

He went on to set up other accounts he used to siphon the victim's funds, ultimately stealing nearly $9.8 million, according to prosecutors, who said some of the money went to a multimillion-dollar home, a $1.4 million beach club membership, and a $340,000 donation to Okuma's church.

Okuma and his lawyer didn't immediately respond to requests for comment. In a sentencing memorandum filed earlier this month, Okuma had requested a prison term of six years and six months, the lowest possible sentence under his plea agreement. That memo acknowledged that Okuma had "committed a serious offense, and he deserves to be punished." The memo also noted that he had no previous criminal record, and that before the Justice Department charged him in the present case, Okuma had "owned up to his inexcusable conduct, surrendered his professional licenses, and made unprecedented efforts towards restitution-efforts which resulted in the return of approximately $2.8 million dollars."

The Justice Department partly disputed that characterization, writing in its own sentencing memo that while Okuma had taken "taken steps to correct his wrongs, when his scheme first began to fall apart, his immediate reaction was to falsely blame [the victim's] caregiver, rather than take responsibility himself." Prosecutors sought a sentence of eight years and one month, the maximum allowable under the plea agreement.
A federal judge in Georgia's Northern District opted for a sentence of seven years and four months, near the midpoint between the terms the defense and prosecution were seeking.

Earlier this year, Okuma reached a settlement with the Securities and Exchange Commission under which he agreed to pay $13 million to resolve civil charges in the matter. Prosecutors say that Okuma has repaid just over $2 million in the civil case and made a direct payment of slightly more than $800,000 to the victim. Finra, the brokerage sector's self-regulatory authority, barred Okuma from the industry last December after the organization said he refused to cooperate with an investigation.

The fraud began when Okuma was registered as a broker and advisor with Edward Jones and continued when he moved to Equitable Advisors. He resigned from Equitable in June 2025 "after the firm suspended him due to allegations of misappropriation by a non-Equitable Advisors' client," according to the online database BrokerCheck.
